Based on the provided healthcare Q&A matches, here is a synthesized clear and concise answer to the user's question:

The user inquires about comparing the long-term results of two surgical approaches for high-degree hernias: transanal pull-through and transabdominal pull-through. While both procedures are considered minimally invasive, there is evidence suggesting that the transabdominal approach may have better long-term outcomes.

A review of the retrieved matches indicates that studies have shown improved continence scores and reduced enterocolitis and stool pattern abnormalities in patients treated with the abdominal approach (termed "TERPT group"). In contrast, the TALP group (transanal pull-through) has been associated with somewhat better stool patterns and a lower incidence of enterocolitis.

Furthermore, research suggests that the transabdominal approach may provide more reliable fixation and improved wound healing compared to the transanal approach. However, this is still an area under investigation, and more studies are needed to confirm these findings.

While there is limited evidence to suggest that the two approaches have equivalent long-term outcomes, the data suggest that the abdominal approach may offer better short-term results due to its potentially superior fixation and wound healing properties. Ultimately, the choice of surgical approach will depend on individual patient factors, including hernia size, location, and medical history.

It is essential to note that these findings are based on a limited number of studies and require further investigation to confirm these observations. Patients considering surgery for high-degree hernias should discuss their specific situation with their healthcare provider to determine the most appropriate treatment option.
